1	# DeepSeek-V2: Efficient MoE Language Model with Multi-Head Latent Attention
     2	
     3	## Source
     4	https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04434
     5	
     6	## Model Overview
     7	
     8	DeepSeek-V2 is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model with 236B total parameters, of which only 21B are activated per token. It supports a 128K-token context length. The model was pretrained on 8.1T tokens from a high-quality, multi-source corpus with extended Chinese data. Post-training includes Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on 1.5M conversational sessions and Reinforcement Learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).
     9	
    10	Compared with DeepSeek 67B (a dense predecessor), DeepSeek-V2 delivers:
    11	- **42.5% reduction** in training costs
    12	- **93.3% reduction** in KV cache size
    13	- **5.76× higher** maximum generation throughput
    14	
    15	## Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA)
    16	
    17	Conventional Multi-Head Attention (MHA) stores full key-value pairs per head per token, creating a KV cache bottleneck during autoregressive generation. Alternatives like Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) and Multi-Query Attention (MQA) reduce cache but sacrifice performance.
    18	
    19	MLA introduces **low-rank key-value joint compression**: instead of caching full K and V vectors, MLA compresses them into a compact latent vector $\mathbf{c}_t^{KV}$, which is cached during inference. Full keys, values, and a decoupled RoPE-based positional key are reconstructed on-the-fly via learned projection matrices. This yields **better performance than MHA** while requiring dramatically less cache.
    20	
    21	![Attention mechanism comparison: MHA vs GQA vs MQA vs MLA](./assets/figure_2.jpg)
    22	
    23	## DeepSeekMoE Architecture
    24	
    25	The FFN layers use the DeepSeekMoE design with two expert types:
    26	- **Shared experts** ($N_s$): always activated, capture common knowledge
    27	- **Routed experts** ($N_r$): sparsely activated via a top-$K_r$ router
    28	
    29	Fine-grained expert segmentation increases specialization potential. Device-limited routing constrains each token to experts on at most $M$ devices, reducing cross-node communication. Auxiliary losses enforce load balance across experts and devices, and a token-dropping strategy during training prevents expert overflow without affecting inference.
    30	
    31	![DeepSeek-V2 architecture diagram](./assets/figure_1.jpg)
    32	
    33	## Performance Benchmarks
    34	
    35	DeepSeek-V2 achieves top-tier MMLU performance among open-source models while activating far fewer parameters than competitors.
    36	
    37	| Model | Activated Params (B) | MMLU Score |
    38	|---|---|---|
    39	| DeepSeek-V2 | 21 | 78.5 |
    40	| LLaMA 3 70B | 70 | 77.0 |
    41	| Mixtral 8x22B | 39 | 77.6 |
    42	| Qwen1.5 72B | 72 | 75.6 |
    43	| DeepSeek 67B | 67 | 73.0 |
    44	| LLaMA 2 70B | 70 | 69.0 |
    45	| Mixtral 8x7B | 13 | 70.6 |
    46	| LLaMA 3 8B | 8 | 65.0 |
    47	
    48	![MMLU vs activated parameters](./assets/figure_3.jpg)
    49	
    50	## Alignment and Chat Evaluation
    51	
    52	After SFT and GRPO-based RL, DeepSeek-V2 Chat (RL) achieves strong results on open-ended conversation benchmarks:
    53	
    54	| Benchmark | DeepSeek-V2 Chat (RL) |
    55	|---|---|
    56	| AlpacaEval 2.0 (length-controlled win rate) | 38.9% |
    57	| MT-Bench (overall) | 8.97 |
    58	| AlignBench (overall, Chinese) | 7.91 |
    59	
    60	On AlignBench (Chinese), DeepSeek-V2 Chat (RL) outperforms all open-source models and most closed-source models, demonstrating exceptional multilingual alignment quality.
    61	
    62	## Key Findings
    63	
    64	- **MLA achieves superior performance to MHA** while reducing KV cache by 93.3%, making it a strictly better alternative to GQA/MQA for inference efficiency.
    65	- **DeepSeekMoE with fine-grained experts and shared expert isolation** enables training a 236B-parameter model at 42.5% lower cost than a 67B dense model.
    66	- **Only 21B activated parameters** are needed to match or exceed 70B-class dense models (LLaMA 3 70B, Qwen1.5 72B) on MMLU.
    67	- **5.76× throughput improvement** over DeepSeek 67B makes DeepSeek-V2 practical for large-scale deployment.
    68	- **DeepSeek-V2 Chat (RL) is the strongest open-source chat model in Chinese** and competitive with closed-source systems in English open-ended evaluation.

     6	
     7	## 1. SVG Banned Features Blacklist
     8	
     9	The following features are **absolutely forbidden** when generating SVGs — PPT export will break if any are used:
    10	
    11	| Banned Feature | Description |
    12	|----------------|-------------|
    13	| `clipPath` | Clipping paths |
    14	| `mask` | Masks |
    15	| `<style>` | Embedded stylesheets |
    16	| `class` | CSS selector attributes (`id` inside `<defs>` is a legitimate reference and is NOT banned) |
    17	| External CSS | External stylesheet links |
    18	| `<foreignObject>` | Embedded external content |
    19	| `<symbol>` + `<use>` | Symbol reference reuse |
    20	| `textPath` | Text along a path |
    21	| `@font-face` | Custom font declarations |
    22	| `<animate*>` / `<set>` | SVG animations |
    23	| `<script>` / event attributes | Scripts and interactivity |
    24	| `marker` / `marker-end` | Line endpoint markers |
    25	| `<iframe>` | Embedded frames |

    28	
    29	## 2. PPT Compatibility Alternatives

    35	| `<image opacity="0.3"/>` | Overlay a `<rect fill="background-color" opacity="0.7"/>` mask layer after the image |
    36	| `marker-end` arrows | Draw triangle arrows with `<polygon>` |

    38	**Mnemonic**: PPT does not recognize rgba, group opacity, image opacity, or markers.

    70	## 4. Basic SVG Rules
    71	
    72	- **viewBox** must match the canvas dimensions (`width`/`height` must match `viewBox`)

    74	- **Line breaks**: Use `<tspan>` for manual line breaks; `<foreignObject>` is FORBIDDEN

   108	## 6. Shadow & Overlay Techniques
   109	
   110	> `<mask>` elements and `<image opacity="...">` are banned. Always use stacked `<rect>` or gradient overlays instead (see §2).
   111	
   112	### Shadow
   113	
   114	#### Filter Soft Shadow — Recommended
   115	
   116	Best for: cards, floating panels, elevated elements. `svg_to_shapes.py` automatically converts `feGaussianBlur` + `feOffset` into native PPTX `<a:outerShdw>`.
   117	
   118	```xml
   119	<defs>
   120	  <filter id="softShadow" x="-15%" y="-15%" width="140%" height="140%">
   121	    <feGaussianBlur in="SourceAlpha" stdDeviation="8"/>
   122	    <feOffset dx="0" dy="4" result="offsetBlur"/>
   123	    <feFlood flood-color="#000000" flood-opacity="0.08" result="shadowColor"/>
   124	    <feComposite in="shadowColor" in2="offsetBlur" operator="in" result="shadow"/>
   125	    <feMerge>
   126	      <feMergeNode in="shadow"/>
   127	      <feMergeNode in="SourceGraphic"/>
   128	    </feMerge>
   129	  </filter>
   130	</defs>
   131	<rect x="60" y="60" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#FFFFFF" filter="url(#softShadow)"/>
   132	```
   133	
   134	Recommended parameters:
   135	```
   136	stdDeviation:   6–10     (smaller = crisper, larger = softer)
   137	flood-opacity:  0.06–0.12  (keep low for a premium feel)
   138	dy:             3–6      (vertical > horizontal for natural top-light)
   139	dx:             0–2
   140	```
   141	
   142	#### Colored Shadow
   143	
   144	Best for: accent buttons, brand-colored cards. Use the element's own color family instead of black.
   145	
   146	```xml
   147	<filter id="colorShadow" x="-15%" y="-15%" width="140%" height="140%">
   148	  <feGaussianBlur in="SourceAlpha" stdDeviation="10"/>
   149	  <feOffset dx="0" dy="6" result="offsetBlur"/>
   150	  <feFlood flood-color="#1A73E8" flood-opacity="0.20" result="shadowColor"/>
   151	  <feComposite in="shadowColor" in2="offsetBlur" operator="in" result="shadow"/>
   152	  <feMerge>
   153	    <feMergeNode in="shadow"/>
   154	    <feMergeNode in="SourceGraphic"/>
   155	  </feMerge>
   156	</filter>
   157	```
   158	
   159	Replace `flood-color` with the element's brand color; keep `flood-opacity` between 0.12–0.20.
   160	
   161	#### Layered Rect Shadow — High-Compatibility Fallback
   162	
   163	Best for: maximum compatibility with older PowerPoint versions. Stack 2–3 semi-transparent rectangles behind the main card:
   164	
   165	```xml
   166	<!-- Shadow layers (back to front, largest offset first) -->
   167	<rect x="68" y="72" width="400" height="240" rx="16" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="0.03"/>
   168	<rect x="65" y="69" width="400" height="240" rx="14" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="0.05"/>
   169	<rect x="62" y="66" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#1A73E8" fill-opacity="0.04"/>
   170	<!-- Main card -->
   171	<rect x="60" y="60" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#FFFFFF"/>
   172	```
   173	
   174	### Image Overlay
   175	
   176	#### Linear Gradient Overlay — Most Common
   177	
   178	Best for: image+text pages. Gradient direction should match text position (text on left → gradient darkens toward left).
   179	
   180	```xml
   181	<image href="..." x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"/>
   182	<defs>
   183	  <linearGradient id="imgOverlay" x1="0" y1="0" x2="1" y2="0">
   184	    <stop offset="0%"   stop-color="#1A1A2E" stop-opacity="0.85"/>
   185	    <stop offset="55%"  stop-color="#1A1A2E" stop-opacity="0.30"/>
   186	    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#1A1A2E" stop-opacity="0"/>
   187	  </linearGradient>
   188	</defs>
   189	<rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" fill="url(#imgOverlay)"/>
   190	```
   191	
   192	#### Bottom Gradient Bar
   193	
   194	Best for: cover slides and full-image pages with bottom title.
   195	
   196	```xml
   197	<defs>
   198	  <linearGradient id="bottomBar" x1="0" y1="0" x2="0" y2="1">
   199	    <stop offset="0%"   stop-color="#000000" stop-opacity="0"/>
   200	    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#000000" stop-opacity="0.72"/>
   201	  </linearGradient>
   202	</defs>
   203	<rect x="0" y="380" width="1280" height="340" fill="url(#bottomBar)"/>
   204	```
   205	
   206	#### Radial Gradient Overlay — Vignette Effect
   207	
   208	Best for: full-screen atmosphere slides; draws attention to the center.
   209	
   210	```xml
   211	<defs>
   212	  <radialGradient id="vignette" cx="50%" cy="50%" r="70%">
   213	    <stop offset="0%"   stop-color="#000000" stop-opacity="0"/>
   214	    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#000000" stop-opacity="0.58"/>
   215	  </radialGradient>
   216	</defs>
   217	<rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" fill="url(#vignette)"/>
   218	```
   219	
   220	#### Brand Color Overlay
   221	
   222	Best for: slides needing strong visual brand identity.
   223	
   224	```xml
   225	<defs>
   226	  <linearGradient id="brandOverlay" x1="0" y1="0" x2="1" y2="0">
   227	    <stop offset="0%"   stop-color="#005587" stop-opacity="0.80"/>
   228	    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#005587" stop-opacity="0.10"/>
   229	  </linearGradient>
   230	</defs>
   231	<rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" fill="url(#brandOverlay)"/>
   232	```
   233	
   234	### Quick-Reference Table
   235	
   236	| Scenario | Recommended Technique | Avoid |
   237	|----------|-----------------------|-------|
   238	| Card / panel shadow | Filter soft shadow (`flood-opacity` ≤ 0.12) | Hard black shadow |
   239	| Accent / CTA button | Colored shadow (same hue family) | Generic gray shadow |
   240	| Text over image | Linear gradient overlay (direction matches text side) | Uniform flat opacity over whole image |
   241	| Cover / full-image slide | Bottom gradient bar + brand color | Solid black overlay |
   242	| Atmosphere / hero slide | Radial vignette | Unprocessed raw image |
   243	| Max PPT compatibility needed | Layered rect shadow | Filter-based shadow |

     5	---
     6	
     7	## Role Definition
     8	
     9	A creative, versatile-style SVG design executor. Suitable for product introductions, training materials, proposal presentations, marketing campaigns, and other **non-consulting** scenarios. Emphasizes visual impact and information engagement, striking a balance between professionalism and approachability.
    10	
    11	---
    12	
    13	## General-specific Layout Techniques
    14	
    15	### 1. Flexible and Varied Layouts
    16	
    17	The General style is not confined to fixed templates; layouts can be freely chosen based on content:
    18	
    19	| Layout | Use Case | Layout Details (1280x720) |
    20	|--------|----------|--------------------------|
    21	| Full-image background + text overlay | Covers, emotional pages | `<image>` fills canvas + semi-transparent overlay + centered title |
    22	| Left-right split (image-text mix) | Feature introductions, comparisons | Left x=40,w=580 / Right x=660,w=580 |
    23	| Three-column cards | Feature lists, team introductions | x=40,450,860 each w=380, equal-height cards |
    24	| Top-bottom split | Timelines, process flows | Top area: title+description h=250 / Bottom area: charts+content h=420 |
    25	| Center-radiating | Core concepts, ecosystem diagrams | Center element + 4-6 surrounding nodes, lines pointing to center |
    26	| Waterfall / Z-pattern | Storytelling, case studies | Content blocks alternate left-right, guiding the eye in a Z-pattern |
    27	
    28	### 2. Visual Rhythm Control
    29	
    30	- **Information density alternation**: Follow a data-heavy page with a "breathing page" (large image / quote / transition) to prevent audience fatigue
    31	- **Visual weight balance**: Dark/large-area elements are "heavy", light/small elements are "light" — balance left-right/top-bottom
    32	- **Repetition and variation**: Maintain layout consistency within a chapter; vary between chapters to maintain freshness
    33	
    34	### 3. Decorative Element Usage
    35	
    36	| Element | Usage | Notes |
    37	|---------|-------|-------|
    38	| Gradient blocks | Background zones, title backing | Use `<linearGradient>` / `<radialGradient>`, limit to 2-3 colors |
    39	| Rounded rectangle cards | Content containers, feature modules | `rx="12"` with light shadow (simulate with lighter rect) |
    40	| Icon accents | List item prefixes, feature markers | Use `data-icon` placeholders, size 32-48px |
    41	| Numbered circles | Step flows, ranked lists | `<circle>` + centered `<text>`, theme color fill |
    42	| Divider lines | Content separation | `<line>` or `<rect height="2">`, opacity 0.2-0.3 |
    43	
    44	---
    45	
    46	## Visual Strategy
    47	
    48	### Color Usage
    49	
    50	- **Bold use of theme color**: Covers and chapter pages can use large areas of theme color background
    51	- **Gradients enhance depth**: Title bars and card backgrounds can use same-hue gradients
    52	- **Contrast creates focus**: Key numbers/words use accent color, creating contrast with surroundings
    53	- **Color-mood matching**: Cool tones for tech feel, warm tones for energy, dark tones for gravitas
    54	
    55	### Image Handling Strategy
    56	
    57	| Scenario | Strategy | SVG Implementation |
    58	|----------|----------|-------------------|
    59	| Full-screen background | Image fills + dark gradient overlay | `preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"` + gradient rect |
    60	| Portrait image display | Place left/right, maintain original ratio | Control width, height adapts |
    61	| Multi-image grid | Grid arrangement, uniform sizing | Equal-width equal-height `<image>` matrix |
    62	| Person photo | Circular crop effect | `<circle>` background + square image overlay (post-processing crops) |
    63	
    64	### Typography Hierarchy
    65	
    66	```
    67	Title layer   → 28-36px, bold, theme color or white
    68	Subtitle layer → 20-24px, medium weight, secondary color
    69	Body layer    → 16-18px, regular, dark gray
    70	Annotation layer → 12-14px, light gray, bottom-aligned
    71	```
    72	
    73	---
    74	
    75	## Speaker Notes Style
    76	
    77	### Narrative Tone
    78	
    79	General style speaker notes use **conversational narration** — like talking with the audience, not reading a report. Natural tone with rhythm, using rhetorical devices where appropriate.
    80	
    81	### Stage Direction Markers
    82	
    83	| Marker | Purpose | Example |
    84	|--------|---------|---------|
    85	| `[Pause]` | Silence after key reveal, letting the audience absorb | "What does this number mean? [Pause] It means 1 in every 3 users..." |
    86	| `[Interactive]` | Ask questions or guide audience participation | "[Interactive] How many of you have used this feature?" |
    87	| `[Transition]` | Bridge from previous page, must be at start of each page's text | "[Transition] Now that we understand the context, let's see how it works." |
    88	
    89	### Notes Writing Guidelines
    90	
    91	- **Tell stories**: Use "scenario-conflict-resolution" structure for each page's narrative
    92	- **Use metaphors**: Make abstract concepts tangible ("It's like adding a turbocharger to the system")
    93	- **Create suspense**: Pose questions at the right time, answer on the next page
    94	- **Conversational data**: 30% → "nearly one-third", 2.5x → "more than doubled"
    95	- **Key points structure**: `Key points: (1) Core message (2) Supporting evidence (3) Call to action`
    96	
    97	### Notes Example
    98	
    99	```markdown
   100	# 03_key_advantages
   101	
   102	[Transition] Having covered the market landscape, you might be wondering: where is our opportunity?
   103	
   104	Our core advantages can be summed up in three words: Fast, Accurate, Efficient.
   105	Fast — deployment time cut from 3 months to 2 weeks; [Pause]
   106	Accurate — recognition accuracy at 97.3%, far exceeding the industry average of 82%;
   107	Efficient — overall costs reduced by nearly one-third.
   108	
   109	[Interactive] If you were the decision-maker, which of these three numbers would impress you most?
   110	
   111	Key points: (1) Three differentiating advantages (2) Quantitative data support (3) Prompt for reflection
   112	Duration: 2 minutes
   113	```

| **Use Case** | Technical research paper presentation on DeepSeek-V2 architecture and efficiency |

---

## II. Canvas Specification

| Property | Value |
| -------- | ----- |
| **Format** | PPT 16:9 |
| **Dimensions** | 1280 x 720 px |
| **viewBox** | `0 0 1280 720` |

| **Content Area** | x: 60-1220, y: 100-670 |
| **Title Area** | y: 50-100 |
| **Grid Base** | 40px |

---

## III. Visual Theme

### Theme Style

- **Style**: Anthropic (tech-forward, professional, modern, conclusion-first)
- **Theme**: Mixed (dark cover/chapter + light content pages)
- **Tone**: Technical, data-forward, concise — matching the research paper presentation style

### Color Scheme

| Role | HEX | Purpose |
| ---- | --- | ------- |
| **Background (dark)** | `#1A1A2E` | Cover/chapter dark backgrounds |
| **Background (light)** | `#FFFFFF` | Content page backgrounds |
| **Secondary bg** | `#F8FAFC` | Card backgrounds, panels |
| **Primary** | `#D97757` | Anthropic Orange — titles, emphasis, key data, top bars |
| **Accent** | `#4A90D9` | Tech Blue — charts, links, architecture diagrams |
| **Secondary accent** | `#10B981` | Mint Green — positive indicators, success states, recommended options |
| **Body text** | `#1A1A2E` | Main body text on light pages |
| **Secondary text** | `#64748B` | Captions, annotations, chart labels |
| **Tertiary text** | `#94A3B8` | Footers, supplementary info |
| **Border/divider** | `#E2E8F0` | Card borders, divider lines |
| **Success** | `#10B981` | Positive trend indicators |
| **Warning** | `#EF4444` | Risks, cautions (Coral Red) |
| **Dark text on dark bg** | `#FFFFFF` | White text on dark backgrounds |

### Gradient Scheme

```xml
<!-- Dark background gradient -->
<linearGradient id="bgGradient" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="100%">
  <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#1A1A2E"/>
  <stop offset="50%" stop-color="#16213E"/>
  <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#0F0F1A"/>
</linearGradient>

<!-- Orange accent gradient -->
<linearGradient id="accentGradient" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="0%">
  <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#D97757"/>
  <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#E8956F"/>
</linearGradient>

<!-- Card gradient -->
<linearGradient id="cardGradient" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="0%" y2="100%">
  <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#FFFFFF"/>
  <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#F8FAFC"/>
</linearGradient>
```

---

## IV. Typography System

### Font Plan

**Recommended preset**: P5 (English-primary)

| Role | Chinese | English | Fallback |
| ---- | ------- | ------- | -------- |
| **Title** | Microsoft YaHei | Arial | Helvetica Neue, Segoe UI, sans-serif |
| **Body** | Microsoft YaHei | Calibri | Georgia, Times, serif |
| **Code** | - | Consolas | Monaco, monospace |
| **Emphasis** | SimHei | Arial Black | Arial, sans-serif |

**Font stack**: `Arial, "Helvetica Neue", "Segoe UI", sans-serif`

### Font Size Hierarchy

**Baseline**: Body font size = 18px (dense technical content, 6+ items per page)

| Purpose | Ratio | Size | Weight |
| ------- | ----- | ---- | ------ |
| Cover title | 3x | 54px | Bold |
| Page title | 1.8x | 32px | Bold |
| Subtitle | 1.3x | 24px | SemiBold |
| Card title | 1.2x | 22px | Bold |
| **Body content** | **1x** | **18px** | Regular |
| Data highlight | 2.2x | 40px | Bold |
| Annotation | 0.75x | 14px | Regular |
| Page number/date | 0.65x | 12px | Regular |
| Label | 0.75x | 14px | 500 |

---

## V. Layout Principles

### Page Structure

- **Header area**: y=0-100 (top orange bar 6px, page label, page title)
- **Content area**: y=110-660 (main content, cards, charts)
- **Footer area**: y=670-720 (page number centered, source info)

### Common Layout Modes

| Mode | Suitable Scenarios |
| ---- | ----------------- |
| **Single column centered** | Cover, takeaways, conclusion |
| **Left-right split (5:5)** | Comparisons (efficiency gains slide) |
| **Left-right split (4:6)** | Image-text mix (architecture, MLA mechanism) |
| **Top-bottom split** | Processes, chart + text |
| **Three column cards** | Feature lists, key findings |
| **Matrix grid** | Comparative analysis |

### Spacing Specification

| Element | Recommended Range | Current Project |
| ------- | ---------------- | --------------- |
| Card gap | 20-32px | 30px |
| Content block gap | 24-40px | 30px |
| Card padding | 20-32px | 24px |
| Card border radius | 8-16px | 12px |
| Icon-text gap | 8-16px | 12px |
| Single-row card height | 530-600px | 520px |
| Double-row card height | 265-295px each | 280px |
| Three-column card width | 360-380px each | 370px |

---

## VI. Icon Usage Specification

### Source

- **Built-in icon library**: `templates/icons/` (640+ icons)
- **Usage method**: Placeholder format `<use data-icon="icon-name" .../>`

## VII. Chart Reference List

| `kpi_cards` | `templates/charts/kpi_cards.svg` | Slide 06 — efficiency metrics comparison |

- **Layout**: Light content page, two-column text + icon accents (template: 03_content.svg)
- **Title**: The LLM Scaling Dilemma: Performance vs. Training Cost and Inference Speed
- **Content**:
  - Left column — The Problem:
    - Larger models yield better intelligence but incur prohibitive training costs
    - KV cache bottleneck during autoregressive generation limits throughput
    - Dense models waste computation on every token
  - Right column — The Opportunity:
    - MoE architectures activate only a subset of parameters per token
    - Efficient attention mechanisms can compress KV cache without sacrificing quality
    - DeepSeek-V2 combines both approaches for Pareto-optimal scaling

### Part 2: Architecture

#### Slide 03 - Architecture Overview (architecture-overview)
- **Layout**: Light content page, left image + right text (template: 03_content.svg, free layout in content area)
- **Title**: DeepSeek-V2 Architecture: MLA + DeepSeekMoE in a Transformer Block
- **Content**:
  - Left: Reference architecture diagram (figure_1.jpg)
  - Right: Key components

#### Slide 04 - MLA Mechanism (mla-mechanism)
- **Layout**: Light content page, left image + right text (template: 03_content.svg)
- **Title**: Multi-Head Latent Attention Compresses KV Cache by 93.3%
- **Content**:
  - Left: Attention comparison diagram (figure_2.jpg)
  - Right:
    - Problem: MHA stores full K/V per head per token → massive cache
    - GQA/MQA reduce cache but sacrifice performance
    - MLA solution: low-rank key-value joint compression into latent vector c_t^KV
    - Full K/V reconstructed on-the-fly via learned projections
    - Decoupled RoPE-based positional key
    - Result: better performance than MHA with 93.3% less cache

#### Slide 05 - DeepSeekMoE (deepseek-moe)
- **Layout**: Light content page, three-column cards (template: 03_content.svg, free layout)
- **Title**: DeepSeekMoE: Fine-Grained Experts with Shared Expert Isolation
- **Content**:
  - Card 1 — Expert Types:
    - Shared experts (N_s): always activated, capture common knowledge
    - Routed experts (N_r): sparsely activated via top-K_r router
  - Card 2 — Specialization:
    - Fine-grained expert segmentation increases specialization
    - Device-limited routing: token → experts on at most M devices
    - Reduces cross-node communication overhead
  - Card 3 — Training Stability:
    - Auxiliary losses enforce load balance across experts and devices
    - Token-dropping strategy prevents expert overflow during training
    - No inference impact

    <text x="90" y="290" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#64748B">Training a 70B+ dense model demands thousands of GPUs</text>
    <text x="90" y="312" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#64748B">for weeks — costs measured in millions of dollars.</text>

    <text x="685" y="247" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" fill="#64748B">Cache grows linearly with layers × heads × dim.</text>

# 01_title_slide

Welcome to this technical overview of DeepSeek-V2, a groundbreaking Mixture-of-Experts language model that redefines the cost-performance frontier in large language models. DeepSeek-V2 introduces two core architectural innovations — Multi-Head Latent Attention and DeepSeekMoE — that together enable training a 236B-parameter model with only 21B activated per token, while supporting a 128K-token context window. This presentation is based on the paper arXiv:2405.04434.

Key points: (1) Introduce DeepSeek-V2 and its key stats (2) Preview the two main innovations (3) Set expectations for the technical depth
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 02_motivation

[Transition] Before diving into the architecture, let's understand why DeepSeek-V2 was necessary in the first place.

The LLM scaling dilemma is straightforward but painful: larger models yield better intelligence, but they come with prohibitive training costs and slow inference due to KV cache bottlenecks. Dense models like LLaMA 70B or Qwen 72B waste enormous computation because every FFN parameter is activated for every single token. On the attention side, standard Multi-Head Attention stores full key-value pairs per head per token, causing the KV cache to explode during autoregressive generation. The opportunity is clear: MoE architectures can activate only a subset of parameters per token, and efficient attention mechanisms can compress the KV cache without sacrificing quality. DeepSeek-V2 combines both approaches to achieve what we call Pareto-optimal scaling — better performance at lower cost.

Key points: (1) Frame the cost-performance dilemma (2) Identify KV cache and dense FFN as bottlenecks (3) Introduce MoE + efficient attention as the solution path
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 03_architecture

[Transition] So how does DeepSeek-V2 actually work? Let's look at the high-level architecture.

DeepSeek-V2's Transformer block has two key substitutions: MLA replaces standard Multi-Head Attention, and DeepSeekMoE replaces the dense FFN. The rest of the Transformer stack remains familiar — pre-norm, residual connections, and so on. What makes this remarkable is the scale: 236 billion total parameters, but only 21 billion are activated for any given token. It also supports a 128K-token context window and was pretrained on 8.1 trillion tokens. The architecture diagram on the left shows how these two innovations fit together within a single block. MLA handles the attention path with dramatically reduced cache, while DeepSeekMoE handles the feed-forward path with sparse expert activation.

Key points: (1) Show MLA + DeepSeekMoE as drop-in replacements (2) Emphasize 236B total / 21B activated ratio (3) Reference the architecture diagram
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 04_mla_mechanism

[Transition] Let's zoom into the first innovation: Multi-Head Latent Attention, or MLA.

Standard Multi-Head Attention stores full K and V vectors for every head and every token. This creates a massive KV cache that becomes the primary bottleneck during autoregressive generation. Grouped-Query Attention and Multi-Query Attention were proposed as solutions, but they reduce cache at the cost of representational capacity — they sacrifice performance. MLA takes a fundamentally different approach: instead of caching full K and V vectors, it compresses them into a compact latent vector c_t^KV using low-rank joint compression. During inference, full keys and values are reconstructed on-the-fly via learned projection matrices. A decoupled RoPE-based positional key preserves positional information. The result is remarkable: MLA achieves better performance than standard MHA while reducing the KV cache by 93.3%. This makes it strictly superior to both GQA and MQA.

Key points: (1) Explain MHA cache problem (2) Contrast GQA/MQA trade-offs (3) Detail MLA's low-rank compression + decoupled RoPE (4) Emphasize "better than MHA" result
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 05_deepseek_moe

[Transition] Now let's examine the second innovation: DeepSeekMoE, the sparse expert architecture powering the FFN layers.

DeepSeekMoE uses two types of experts. Shared experts are always activated — they capture common, universal knowledge that every token needs. Routed experts are sparsely activated via a top-K_r router, with each token selecting only the most relevant specialists. Fine-grained expert segmentation increases specialization potential: smaller, more numerous experts each master a narrow knowledge niche. To control communication overhead, device-limited routing constrains each token to experts on at most M devices, bounding all-to-all communication. Training stability is ensured through auxiliary load-balancing losses that prevent expert collapse, and a token-dropping strategy that handles overflow during training without affecting inference.

Key points: (1) Shared vs routed experts (2) Fine-grained segmentation and device-limited routing (3) Load balancing and token dropping for stability
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 06_efficiency_gains

[Transition] These architectural innovations translate into concrete, measurable efficiency gains. Here are the three headline numbers, all relative to the dense predecessor DeepSeek 67B.

First, training cost is reduced by 42.5%. This comes directly from MoE sparsity and shared expert isolation — we're training a 236B-parameter model more cheaply than a 67B dense model. Second, KV cache size is reduced by 93.3%, thanks to MLA's low-rank compression replacing full key-value storage. Third, maximum generation throughput improves by 5.76×, driven by the combination of a smaller cache and sparse FFN activation. These are not marginal improvements — they represent a step change in the economics of training and serving large language models.

Key points: (1) 42.5% training cost reduction (2) 93.3% KV cache reduction (3) 5.76× throughput improvement (4) All relative to DeepSeek 67B
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 07_mmlu_performance

[Transition] Efficiency is meaningless without performance. Let's look at how DeepSeek-V2 competes on MMLU, the standard benchmark for reasoning and knowledge.

This scatter plot shows MMLU score on the Y-axis against activated parameters on the X-axis. DeepSeek-V2 sits at 78.5 MMLU with only 21 billion activated parameters — the highest score among all open-source models shown, at the lowest activated parameter count. Compare this to LLaMA 3 70B at 77.0 with 70B active, Mixtral 8×22B at 77.6 with 39B active, and Qwen1.5 72B at 75.6 with 72B active. DeepSeek-V2 is Pareto-optimal: no other model achieves higher MMLU with fewer activated parameters. The dashed orange line traces the efficiency frontier, and DeepSeek-V2 sits clearly above it.

Key points: (1) DeepSeek-V2: 78.5 MMLU at 21B active (2) Compare to LLaMA 3 70B, Mixtral, Qwen (3) Emphasize Pareto-optimal positioning
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 08_alignment_results

[Transition] Beyond pretraining benchmarks, DeepSeek-V2 also excels after alignment through SFT and RL.

The alignment pipeline consists of supervised fine-tuning on 1.5 million conversational sessions, followed by reinforcement learning using Group Relative Policy Optimization — GRPO. The chat-tuned model, DeepSeek-V2 Chat (RL), achieves strong results across open-ended conversation benchmarks. On AlpacaEval 2.0, it reaches a 38.9% length-controlled win rate. On MT-Bench, it scores 8.97 overall. Most notably, on AlignBench — the Chinese open-ended conversation benchmark — it scores 7.91, outperforming all open-source models and most closed-source models. This demonstrates exceptional multilingual alignment quality, particularly for Chinese-language applications.

Key points: (1) SFT + GRPO alignment pipeline (2) Three benchmark scores (3) Chinese leadership on AlignBench
Duration: 1.5 minutes

---

# 09_takeaways

[Transition] To conclude, here are the five key takeaways from DeepSeek-V2.

First, MLA is a strictly better alternative to GQA and MQA — it achieves superior performance while reducing KV cache by 93.3%. Second, DeepSeekMoE with fine-grained experts and shared expert isolation enables training a 236B-parameter model at 42.5% lower cost than a 67B dense model. Third, only 21 billion activated parameters are needed to match or exceed 70B-class dense models on MMLU — a Pareto-optimal result. Fourth, the 5.76× throughput improvement over DeepSeek 67B makes large-scale deployment practical. And fifth, DeepSeek-V2 Chat (RL) is the strongest open-source chat model in Chinese and competitive with closed-source systems in English. Together, these innovations demonstrate that architectural creativity can unlock efficient scaling without sacrificing capability.

Key points: (1) MLA as new attention standard (2) DeepSeekMoE for economical training (3) Pareto-optimal MMLU (4) Practical deployment throughput (5) Multilingual alignment leadership
Duration: 2 minutes
